content.title: About
content.content: Guava paste is a thick fruit product made from ripe guavas, commonly used in confectionery, desserts, and sauces. The paste has a bright orange color, a sweet‑tart flavor, and the characteristic aroma of guava.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Guava originates from tropical regions of Central and South America, but is now cultivated in Asia and Africa.
Guava contains 4–5 times more vitamin C than oranges.
Guava paste is widely used in Asian cuisine for making marmalades, jellies, and pastry fillings.
Guava is a good source of dietary fiber, which supports digestive health.
Traditional guava paste is made without added sugar, though commercial versions often contain sweeteners.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These nutrients help maintain healthy vision and skin.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes regular digestion and can help regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: Contains folate
items.content: Folate is essential for DNA synthesis and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to guava.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Commercial pastes often contain added sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity of guava can irritate the stomach lining in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Guava paste can be used as a filling for cakes, cupcakes, and cookies, added to smoothies, yogurts, or sauces for meat and seafood, and spread on toast or pancakes. It can also be thinned with a little water or juice for a smoother consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store guava paste in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0 °C–4 °C. Once opened, it typically lasts 2–3 weeks. Discard the product if you notice mold, off‑smell, or off‑taste.

oatmeal-regular-or-quick-made-with-milk-.title: Oatmeal, regular or quick, made with milk, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Oatmeal is made from whole oat grains that can be rolled (regular) or finely cut (quick‑cooking). This version is prepared with milk and contains no added fat, resulting in a creamy and nutrient‑dense breakfast.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Oats are one of the oldest cultivated grains, grown by humans for over 5,000 years.
Rolled, thick‑cut, and instant oats differ mainly in thickness and cooking time.
Cooking with milk boosts calcium and vitamin D content compared with water.
Oats contain beta‑glucans, soluble fibers that help lower cholesterol.
Oatmeal appears in traditional dishes worldwide, from Scottish porridge to Asian sweet congee.

items.title: Rich in beta‑glucans
items.content: Beta‑glucans help regulate blood sugar and reduce cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Provides sustained energy and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1, B5 and folate support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from milk
items.content: Preparing with milk increases calcium for bone health and vitamin D for its absorption.

items.title: Provides magnesium and iron
items.content: These minerals are essential for muscle, nerve, and blood health.

items.title: Allergy to oats or milk
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to oat proteins or milk.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking or fermentation can mitigate this.

items.title: Higher glycemic index for quick oats
items.content: Instant oatmeal may raise blood sugar more rapidly than regular oats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the oatmeal with milk and add fruit, nuts, honey, or spices. It works well as a breakfast, snack, or base for protein smoothies.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry oats in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked oatmeal should be refrigerated and consumed within 2–3 days.

pasta-with-tomato-based-sauce-poultry-an.title: Pasta with tomato-based sauce, poultry, and added vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: A home recipe for pasta cooked with a tomato‑based sauce, pieces of chicken, and added vegetables (carrot, bell pepper, zucchini). The pasta is boiled al dente, while the sauce is slightly spicy and flavored with basil and oregano.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato sauce is a source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.
Chicken provides high‑quality, easily digestible protein.
Adding a variety of vegetables boosts the dish’s vitamin and mineral content.
Traditional pasta with tomato sauce is Italian, but this version adds poultry for extra heartiness.
Homemade sauce lets you control the amount of salt and sugar.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and pasta together supply essential amino acids needed for tissue repair and maintenance.

items.title: Antioxidant properties of tomatoes
items.content: Lycopene in tomatoes helps protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pasta and chicken contain B1, B3, B6, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Fiber and micronutrients
items.content: Vegetables add dietary fiber, vitamin C, potassium, and magnesium, supporting digestion and heart health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When prepared with minimal oil, the dish remains heart‑friendly.

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to poultry.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: If the sauce is salted, monitor overall sodium intake.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Chicken must be fully cooked to avoid salmonella risk.

items.title: Tomato acidity
items.content: People with acid reflux may find tomato sauce irritating.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, mixed with the sauce, chicken, and vegetables. Top with grated Parmesan, fresh basil, or a drizzle of olive oil if desired. The dish stores well in the refrigerator and can be reheated.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cooked pasta in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

rice-white-with-carrots-no-added-fat.title: Rice, white, with carrots, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: White rice with carrots and no added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of boiled white rice and finely diced carrots. It is prepared without oil or other fats, making it low‑calorie and suitable for diet menus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: White rice is one of the most consumed grain foods worldwide.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
The absence of added fats reduces the dish’s calorie count to about 120 kcal per 100 g.
Rice with carrots is traditionally prepared in Asian cuisines as a side dish or soup base.
When stored properly, rice retains its flavor and quality for up to a year.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: White rice provides a quick source of energy through easily digestible carbs.

items.title: Beta‑carotene from carrots
items.content: Beta‑carotene supports vision, immunity, and skin health.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: No added fats make the dish suitable for weight management and cholesterol control.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Carrot fiber promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: White rice can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should monitor portion sizes.

items.title: Low fiber compared to whole grains
items.content: White rice provides less dietary fiber than whole‑grain varieties.

items.title: Carrot allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergic reaction to carrots.

items.title: Arsenic contamination
items.content: In some regions rice may contain elevated arsenic levels; choose reputable suppliers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish with meat or fish, add to salads, soups, or use as a quick meal base. Optional seasonings, herbs, or low‑sodium soy sauce can be added without extra oil.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 2 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before consumption.
